annotations.annotation_text: Page 311 opens Book 2, Chapter 3 ("The Tavern") during the Age of Heroes phase. This passage continues HCE behind the bar at his Chapelizod pub, the Norwegian Captain tale, the television broadcast, the twelve customers drinking and judging, featuring HCE, the Twelve Customers, Butt and Taff. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8
Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com
JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: The Norwegian Captain tale (311.05): pub raconteur story based on an anecdote told by John Stanislaus Joyce. A hunchbacked Norse sea-captain (HCE avatar) arrives in Dublin demanding a bespoke suit from tailor Kersse.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp

annotations.annotation_text: Kersse the Tailor (311.12): German 'Kirsche' (cherry) + kersey wool cloth + French 'caresse' + Irish 'ciar' (dark). Represents native Irish craftsmanship coping with demanding foreign invaders.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 311 ("The Tavern"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: The Ship's Husband (311.20): Philip McCann, Dublin ship's chandler and Joyce's godfather, acting as commercial intermediary and negotiator between the foreign captain and the local tailor.

Historical allegory (311.28): the commercial dispute over tailoring mirrors the historical Norse settlement of Dublin (Dyflin) in the 9th century, exploring how invaders are domesticated through local trade and marriage.
sources: Curtis, Edmund. A History of Ireland. https://archive.org/details/historyofireland0000curt
